query: High-entropy alloys can combine mechanical strength, wear resistance, corrosion protection, oxidation resistance, and thermal stability, while their large compositional space offers opportunities to tune degradation in harsh environments. Prior studies have largely considered wear and corrosion separately, and only a few reports address their combined action, leaving the governing behavior poorly understood. For a high-entropy alloy subjected to tribo-corrosion, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs the coupled response and why? Describe a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, predict changes in total degradation and its wear and corrosion components relative to a matched baseline, state where the prediction should hold or fail, connect it to the available prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys under tribo-corrosion conditions, wear-induced shear not only removes the native passive oxide film but also triggers an in situ transformation—producing an ultra-fine, partially amorphous surface layer with compositional segregation. This mechanically induced compositional heterogeneity compromises the repassivation ability of the surface and forms localized galvanic cells, thereby accelerating pitting and localized corrosion that feed back to further increase wear. In other words, the synergy between shear‐induced phase/amorphization (with segregation) and inadequate repassivation governs the coupled tribo-corrosion degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase or dual-phase high-entropy alloy (e.g., CoCrFeNiMoCu0.1 or a similar alloy with moderate Cr and other passivating elements) in a homogenized, as-processed microstructure with a stable native passive film.
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled ball-on-disk sliding tests in a chloride-containing aqueous medium (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl) under specified normal loads and sliding speeds while comparing with tests in an inert or low-oxygen environment.
generation.conditions: Testing at ambient temperature in a corrosive electrolyte (3.5 wt% NaCl) with defined load cycles (e.g., 5–30 N) and sliding speeds (e.g., 1–10 mm/s). A matched baseline test in either an inert electrolyte or under UHV conditions (to suppress oxidation) will serve as a control for wear-only response.
generation.structural_mediator: Shear-induced amorphization accompanied by localized compositional segregation and defects within the newly formed surface layer, which disrupts the uniformity of the passive film.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, mechanical stresses induce local amorphization and phase segregation at the wear track, creating compositional gradients that degrade the integrity of the continuously repassivated oxide film. These segregated regions act as anodic sites that are more susceptible to chloride attack, leading to accelerated pitting and localized corrosion. The resulting corrosion damage further undermines the mechanical integrity of the surface, reinforcing the wear process in a positive-feedback loop.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to tests in inert environments, tribo-corrosion tests will result in higher localized mass loss, a rougher and more chemically heterogeneous wear track (as revealed by TEM/EDS), and increased variability in friction coefficient and open-circuit potential. The overall degradation (total mass loss) is predicted to be notably higher (e.g., an approximate 50% increase) under coupled conditions.
generation.baseline: The performance of the same HEA under pure wear conditions (in an inert or oxygen-depleted environment) where shear-induced amorphization does occur but without the detrimental effects of active chloride-driven corrosion, resulting in lower mass loss and a more stable passive film.
generation.boundary: This prediction should hold in HEAs whose chemistry allows for shear-induced segregation and where the native oxide film is moderately protective. It may fail in alloys that form extremely robust, self-healing oxide layers (e.g., very high Cr or tailored passivation systems) or in environments where the oxygen content is so low that repassivation and corrosion cannot occur.
generation.uncertainty: The hypothesis integrates observations from studies on shear-induced amorphization and low friction in inert environments (e.g., PMC7311485::web::012::results_and_discussion) with evidence of tribocorrosion performance improvement via stable oxide formation after thermal treatment (e.g., PMC10456374::web::012::3_4_tribocorrosion_performance_after_ann) and the documenting of synergistic corrosion–wear effects (e.g., PMC11378927::web::022::synergistic_effect_between_ce_and_corros). New in this proposal is the link that shear-induced compositional segregation under mechanical loading reduces the reformation quality of the protective film, leading to localized galvanic corrosion. The magnitude and spatial extent of such segregation under realistic tribo-corrosion conditions remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples with identical initial microstructures and native passive films. Subject one set to ball-on-disk sliding tests in 3.5 wt% NaCl under ambient conditions (allowing oxygen and chloride-induced repassivation) and the other set to similar sliding tests in an inert or oxygen-depleted electrolyte. Use real-time OCP monitoring and post-test high-resolution TEM/EDS to analyze the wear track for evidence of amorphous transformation, elemental segregation, and passive film integrity. Compare mass loss, friction coefficient fluctuations, and corrosion pit density between the two sets.
measurements: Friction coefficient and OCP fluctuations (real-time monitoring)
Surface morphology and phase composition (TEM, SEM, and EDS mapping)
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (to assess passive film properties)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear tracks in the corrosive (ambient) test do not exhibit significant compositional segregation, if the passive film integrity remains comparable to the inert condition, or if the total degradation does not markedly exceed that in the inert test (i.e., no significant increase in localized corrosion), then the hypothesis that shear-induced segregation undermines repassivation and accelerates tribo-corrosion is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.4. Tribocorrosion Performance after Annealing in Air Environment
cited_evidence.text: The influence of thermal shock on the tribocorrosion properties of AlCrTiZrMo HEA films is analyzed by monitoring the fluctuation of the OCP and COF of films in the coupled environment of friction and corrosion, as shown in Figure 10. The fluctuation of the OCP and COF of the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film and the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 400 °C, 600 °C and 800 °C for 1 h in air are monitored in real time. In the preparation stage, the samples were completely immersed in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution for 1 h to obtain a stable surface potential. The duration of the whole experiment is 50 min. During the no-load phase of 0–10 min, both the OCP and COF curves remain stable. During the 10–40 min loading stage, the appearance of the activation region causes the OCP curve to drop sharply, then fluctuate around a constant value. During the 40–50 min no-loading stage, the lack of load causes re-passivation within the wear track, and the OCP curve gradually returns to stability. Therefore, OCP can be used as a mixed potential to monitor the passivation state within the wear track [,,].

This work studied an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy that was manufactured using a laser-based consolidation additive manufacturing process. We showed that low friction and high wear resistance are achievable with bare high entropy alloys in inert environments. These characteristics are linked to the shear-induced formation of a highly refined, near-amorphous surface film that exhibits inverse Hall-Petch behavior. The detrimental role of environments, specifically those that result in oxidation, was mitigated by tribological testing in a UHV environment. A newly proposed amorphization model was used to accurately predict the grain size-dependent shear strength, and thus friction coefficient.
